subject: Anthropology
title: Microfinance
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Microfinance.

hook.text: Tiny loans to poor women were supposed to end poverty. Microfinance won a Nobel Prize. But did it actually work?

buildup.text: Microfinance provides small loans to people excluded from formal banking, especially women in developing countries.

discovery.text: Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank showed that the poor are creditworthy. Repayment rates often exceeded traditional banks.

twist.text: Critics found that microfinance often traps borrowers in debt. It can empower individuals but rarely ends poverty.

climax.text: Microfinance reveals a tension: individual solutions can't fix structural problems. Credit without justice isn't enough.

punchline.text: Small loans can't fix big systems.

quiz.question: What is a major critique of microfinance?
options: It can trap borrowers in debt without addressing structural poverty

details.summary: Microfinance provides small loans to poor people excluded from formal banking, aiming to reduce poverty through entrepreneurship. Anthropological research has revealed both successes and serious problems including over-indebtedness, aggressive collection practices.
details.whyItMatters: Microfinance was celebrated as a poverty solution, but ethnographic research has tempered this optimism. Understanding its actual effects on communities reveals the limits of market-based solutions to structural poverty and the dangers of idealizing.
takeaways: Microfinance provides small loans to people excluded from formal banking
It has achieved some successes but also caused over-indebtedness
Ethnographic research reveals the limits of market-based poverty solutions

faq.question: What problems has anthropological research found with microfinance?
faq.answer: Ethnographers have documented over-indebtedness, social pressure on borrowers from group lending, use of loans for consumption rather than investment, aggressive collection practices, and the burden of debt falling disproportionately on women who are the primary targets of microfinance programs.

faq.question: Is microfinance better than traditional aid for reducing poverty?
faq.answer: Research suggests microfinance alone rarely lifts people out of poverty. It helps manage cash flow and emergencies but does not address structural causes of poverty. Randomized trials show modest impacts on income, challenging claims of transformative poverty reduction.
